cells.tense: Present tense — here, with the pen.
cells.verb: setting things right by proportion, not by punishment
cells.place: in the shape of the thing, underneath the particulars
cells.ask: Let one arrangement you can already see is finished actually end — and what comes back is exchange that keeps moving on its own.
cells.core:
You can see where the weight sits. Not in this one conversation or that one invoice — in the whole arrangement, how it tilts, what it would take to level it. And you don't have to count to know. The sense of what's fair arrives already proportioned, and you adjust by it without making a case. Give goes out, receive comes in, and the shape holds.

What that frees up: you can also see when a shape has run its course. Not broken — done. If you wanted, you could let one of those close, cleanly, and see what room it leaves.
cells.sheetLine: You can see what's fair in the shape of things, and you don't need to count to know it.

cells.tense: Future tense — bracing at a future that can't be written in.
cells.verb: levelling every account before it has a chance to settle
cells.place: in a model of how everyone owes everyone, built above the actual people
cells.ask: Carry one unevenness for a week without correcting it — hold it, don't fix it — and what comes back is knowing what's right without running the numbers.
cells.core:
You've worked out the pattern of who gives and who takes, and you're living inside the pattern instead of with the people. Every exchange gets entered somewhere. Every kindness arrives with a column next to it. And some part of you is braced for the day the whole ledger comes due — so you keep squaring it early, before anyone's asked.

The seeing is real. But fairness that has to be enforced in advance isn't fair yet; it's a defense. What you might find: that you can bear a little imbalance without it toppling anything. The capacity to hold a tilt is the thing counting was standing in for.
cells.sheetLine: You've turned a sense of what's fair into a ledger, and you're settling it before anyone asked.

cells.tense: Past tense — still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: letting what's owed to you go unclaimed
cells.place: while seeing the whole slant of it with perfect clarity
cells.ask: Practice one small ask in private, daily, until the words stop catching — and what comes back is taking your share without it feeling like a fight.
cells.core:
You can see exactly how it's uneven. The pattern is plain to you — where the load lands, who it lands on, how it keeps happening. And the clearer you see it, the less you move. Somewhere back there, asking for your share went badly enough that the asking shut down and the seeing kept going, so now you understand the slant perfectly and absorb it anyway.

The way back isn't to force the claim. It's to build the muscle somewhere quieter first — small, repeated, alone, no stakes — until it's just something you do. Steadiness in practice is what makes a claim feel ordinary when it matters.
cells.sheetLine: You see the unfairness clearly, and you've stopped asking for your part of it.

cells.tense: Disowned present — pen down in a room you're already writing.
cells.verb: keeping a tally of what you were given and what you weren't
cells.place: under a theory about how things work that you call neutral
cells.ask: Before the next explanation of how people are, name the one thing you actually wanted — and what comes back is a plain sense of what's right that doesn't need the count.
cells.core:
You'd say you just notice patterns. How people are, how these things tend to go, who ends up carrying what. It sounds like observation. But listen to which patterns you keep noticing: they're the ones where you came up short. The tally is running — it's been running — and it's been dressed as understanding so you never had to call it a grievance.

Underneath the theory there's something simpler and earlier: a direct sense of what mattered to you before you built the explanation around it. That sense doesn't argue. The account is yours. The noticing already knows what it's noticing.
cells.sheetLine: You're counting who got more. You call it seeing how things work.
